strengths: The paper offers a clean conceptual framing that unifies several existing lines of work (TMPD/DPS-variants and optimization-based solvers like DiffPIR/DCDP/DMPlug) under a single 'local MAP' perspective, clarifying when local-MAP updates coincide with posterior-mean-based DPS updates (Gaussian conditional case) and when they diverge.

The 2D Gaussian-mixture toy example (Fig. 3, Appendix A) is a nice, interpretable illustration that concretely shows the mode-seeking vs. mode-averaging behavior of local MAP vs. DPS/DAPS, which supports the qualitative claims made in Sec. 3.2.

Very broad empirical evaluation: 10 image restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet plus 3 scientific inverse-problem benchmarks (LIS, CS-MRI, black hole imaging), with comparisons against a large number of competitive baselines (DPS, DAPS, SITCOM, DiffPIR, DCDP, PnP-DM, RED-diff, etc.).

Strong and fairly consistent quantitative improvements (best in 49/60 image-restoration cases, best PSNR on all scientific tasks), often achieved with lower computational cost/NFEs than the strongest baselines (DAPS, SITCOM), as shown in the runtime ablation (Table 3, Fig. 4).

Practical contributions are useful: an interpretable convex-combination reformulation of the local MAP objective with automatic annealing behavior, and a simple, effective surrogate-gradient trick for non-differentiable forward operators (JPEG, quantization) that is shown to clearly outperform ΠGDM on these tasks.

Reasonable reproducibility support: explicit algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 4), a full hyperparameter table (Table 4) across all 20 task settings, dataset/license details, and extensive qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is fairly thin: the main formal fact used throughout (local MAP = DPS mean iff the conditional posterior p(x0|xt,y) is Gaussian) is an elementary observation, and no result establishes convergence, error bounds, or a precise characterization of when/how much the local-MAP trajectory deviates from either the global MAP or the true posterior in the nonlinear, non-Gaussian regime that dominates the experiments.

The proposed 'probabilistically interpretable' covariance Σ0|t ≈ (k/SNR)I (Sec 4.1) is itself a loose heuristic justified only by qualitative bounds/limits (1)-(3), and the paper explicitly shows it is mathematically equivalent to the heuristic λt-weighted objective used by prior optimization-based methods (Eq. 14 vs Eq. 11 with Σ0|t=λtσy^2 I). The claimed gain in 'interpretability' is therefore largely a re-parameterization; the paper asserts (but does not rigorously ablate) that this reparameterization is what drives the empirical gains.

No direct ablation isolating the effect of the objective reformulation (Eq. 13) versus the mathematically equivalent original formulation (Eq. 14) with well-tuned λt is provided, despite the paper explicitly claiming 'empirical performance strongly depends on our objective reformulation' — this central methodological claim is unverified.

Closely related prior work (Xu et al. [32], which also argues DPS is better understood as MAP estimation, and Gutha et al. [12], which targets global MAP with diffusion priors) is discussed only briefly in related work and is not included as an empirical baseline, despite apparent conceptual overlap with the paper's central thesis.

Some result inconsistencies/possible errors: Table 1 reports unusually large SSIM/LPIPS standard deviations for the Quantization task (e.g., SSIM 0.844±0.467, LPIPS 0.229±0.474), which appear anomalous or possibly mis-tabulated and are not discussed, raising minor concerns about result curation/checking.

The claimed 'best in 49/60 cases' is true but obscures that SITCOM outperforms LMAPS on several ImageNet settings (SR 4×, Inpaint Box, Nonlinear Deblurring); the narrative in the main text emphasizes wins without proportionate discussion of where and why the method underperforms.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: Algorithm 4 and Table 3 refer to the method as 'MAPS' rather than 'LMAPS'; some hyperparameter table entries contain typos (e.g., '0..01' in Table 4); the abstract's headline PSNR gains are cherry-picked from a subset of tasks.

strengths: Provides a clear conceptual framework (local MAP) that unifies and contextualizes existing DPS-family and optimization-based inverse problem solvers (TMPD, DiffPIR, DCDP, etc.), clarifying when local MAP coincides with DPS (Gaussian conditional case) and when it diverges (non-Gaussian/multimodal case), supported by an instructive analytic Gaussian-mixture toy example (Appendix A) that makes the mode-seeking bias explicit.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 10 image restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet and 3 scientific inverse problems (LIS, CS-MRI, black hole imaging), with comparisons against ~15+ baselines, showing consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements and often better computational efficiency (fewer NFEs) than strong baselines like DAPS and SITCOM.

Reasonably rigorous supporting analysis: formal propositions (Appendix B) proving that the posterior covariance of x0 given xt is asymptotically isotropic as t→0, motivating the proposed covariance approximation; a temperature interpretation of the extra hyperparameter k (Appendix C) that adds some principled grounding.

Thorough ablations, including optimization-step vs. NFE trade-offs (Fig. 4), analytical vs. gradient-descent solutions (Table 8), and the effect of the measurement-conditioning strength k2 (Table 10), which help validate design choices and reproducibility of the method.

Transparent and detailed discussion of the relationship to the closely related concurrent work DMAP, explicitly delineating the difference between clean-signal-space and latent-space local MAP formulations.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to DMAP (Xu et al., 2025), which the paper itself describes as 'the closest related work' with 'the same high-level motivation.' The core contribution is largely a change of variable (clean-signal space vs. latent space) plus a covariance approximation and objective reformulation, rather than a fundamentally new inference paradigm, which may be seen as a modest contribution given ICML's bar for originality.

The isotropic covariance approximation is justified only asymptotically (as σ_t^2→0, i.e., near the end of the trajectory), yet it is applied uniformly across the entire diffusion trajectory including large-t regimes where the higher-order anisotropic terms are not necessarily negligible; the paper does not empirically quantify the approximation error at large t.

The additional hyperparameters (k, k1, k2, learning rate, gradient steps) require per-task tuning (Table 4 shows very different values across tasks, e.g., k2 ranging from 0.01 to 30000), undermining the claimed 'interpretability and numerical stability' benefits and raising concerns about practical usability and fair comparison to baselines that use fewer/simpler heuristics.

FID scores are frequently worse than several baselines (including DMAP) despite improved PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, reflecting the well-known reconstruction-vs-realism trade-off of MAP-style estimators; this trade-off is acknowledged only briefly and not analyzed quantitatively (e.g., no diversity or calibration metrics beyond the 2D toy example).

Some baseline numbers appear to be taken directly from other papers (DAPS, InverseBench) rather than being rerun under a controlled, unified experimental protocol, which raises reproducibility and fair-comparison concerns given that hyperparameter tuning and hardware can materially affect reported numbers.

The paper's central theoretical claim—that local MAP is 'a trade-off' between global MAP and posterior sampling—is stated qualitatively but not rigorously quantified (e.g., no bound on the distance between local MAP outputs and either the true posterior samples or the global MAP), leaving the main conceptual contribution somewhat informal.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typo '0..01' in Table 4, dense notation, some repeated baseline/metric paragraphs verbatim in Sections 5.1/5.2) slightly detract from clarity and polish.
